Introduction (2-3 paragraphs)

Starting a Nursing Facility in North Dakota represents a meaningful opportunity to serve elderly and disabled individuals requiring 24-hour skilled nursing care while building a compliant, sustainable care business. The North Dakota market is unique and presents significant challenges and rewards. Oversight and funding are administered by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (ND HHS), with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through North Dakota Medicaid and the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

With a statewide moratorium on new beds through July 2029 and existing facilities operating at approximately 90% occupancy, North Dakota offers a highly regulated and saturated market with significant barriers to entry for new construction. However, this creates a stable environment for well-capitalized operators focused on acquiring and improving existing facilities. With Medicaid reimbursement for swing beds around $399.55 per day and an $8 million annual pool for value-based incentives, the state provides a strong financial framework for providers prepared to navigate licensing, staffing, and rigorous compliance requirements.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Nursing Facility in North Dakota, focusing on the critical path of acquisition. We will cover regulations and licensing, business planning, staffing, reimbursement, and preparing for state and federal inspections.

Table of Contents

  • Understand North Dakota’s Nursing Facility Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand North Dakota’s Nursing Facility Regulations

North Dakota regulates Nursing Facilities through the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (ND HHS), which is responsible for the licensure, regulation, and inspection of all facilities to ensure they meet state and federal standards for patient care, safety, and quality. Given the high prevalence of residents funded by federal programs, providers must also comply with stringent federal frameworks, primarily the regulations set forth by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).

The regulatory framework in North Dakota emphasizes quality of care, resident safety, staffing adequacy, infection control, and compliance with both state administrative codes and federal CMS Conditions of Participation. This includes a deep focus on resident rights, comprehensive care planning, medication management, safety protocols, and robust documentation. Licenses typically require renewal every 1 year, contingent upon a successful annual survey and continued compliance. The current moratorium on new beds makes adherence to these standards even more critical, as your reputation for quality is your primary asset in this market.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

While the primary license is for a “Nursing Facility,” strategic specialization is key to success in North Dakota’s mature market. North Dakota supports multiple service models, each with different staffing, operational, and reimbursement considerations:

  • Traditional Long-Term Skilled Nursing: This is the foundational service for residents who require ongoing, 24/7 medical supervision and assistance with activities of daily living. These facilities serve as a permanent home for many residents.
  • Short-Term Rehabilitation Units: These units focus on post-acute care for patients recovering from surgery, illness, or injury. They offer intensive physical, occupational, and speech therapy with the goal of returning the patient home. This model is heavily reliant on Medicare reimbursement and strong hospital relationships.
  • Specialized Dementia/Alzheimer’s Care Units: These are often secured units within a larger facility, designed with specific environmental and programming features for residents with cognitive impairments. They require specially trained staff and command higher private pay rates or specialized Medicaid reimbursement.
  • Facilities with Swing-Bed Designation: Primarily found in rural areas, these facilities are licensed to “swing” beds between acute hospital care and skilled nursing care levels. This flexibility allows them to meet fluctuating community needs and is supported by specific Medicaid reimbursement rates, such as the ~$399.55/day rate.

Program size in North Dakota typically ranges from 40 to 100+ beds. Due to the moratorium, you cannot build new. Instead, your focus will be on acquiring an existing facility. Demand is strongest for specialized services like dementia/Alzheimer’s care, short-term rehabilitation, and facilities demonstrating superior outcomes through enhanced staffing. Opportunities may exist in acquiring an underperforming facility in any region and transforming its service model and quality of care to meet these high-demand needs.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Given the significant financial investment and liability, providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or Corporation (S-Corp or C-Corp). The first step is to establish your legal business entity. You must:

  • Register your business name and structure with the North Dakota Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS.
  • Secure required insurance coverage, including professional liability, general liability, and workers’ compensation.
  • Submit a licensing application to the ND HHS. In the current market, this will be a Change of Ownership (CHOW) application, which is a complex process involving detailed financial disclosures, operational plans, and proof of capability.

Licensing timelines for a CHOW in North Dakota generally range from 4 to 9 months. This process runs parallel with the CMS certification process (the CMS 855A application), which is also required for the new owner to be able to bill Medicare and Medicaid. The timeline is highly dependent on the readiness of your team and the completeness of your application package. Any errors or omissions can cause significant delays.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is essential for securing financing and guiding your acquisition and operational strategy. Startup costs in North Dakota, which primarily reflect the acquisition price of an existing facility plus working capital, typically range from $2,000,000 to $10,000,000.

Operating expenses are a critical component of your financial projections. These are driven primarily by staffing, which represents approximately 55-65% of total costs in a skilled nursing setting. Other major expenses include mortgage/lease, utilities, raw food, medical supplies, and insurance. Your business plan must detail how you will manage these costs while delivering high-quality care.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges are strong but depend heavily on your payer mix:

  • Medicaid: The primary payer for long-term care. Rates for specific programs like swing beds are around $399.55 per day, with general SNF rates varying.
  • Medicare: The primary payer for short-term rehabilitation. While rates are higher than Medicaid, they are for limited stays. North Dakota facilities see average Medicare margins of around 16%.
  • Value-Based Incentives: North Dakota offers an $8 million annual pool for providers who meet specific quality metrics, providing a significant revenue enhancement opportunity.
  • Private Pay: Residents who pay out-of-pocket, often commanding the highest daily rates.

Providers operating at a target occupancy of 85-90% can achieve sustainable operations, though break-even can take 12 months or more post-acquisition. Profit margins are highly dependent on payer mix and operational efficiency, with strong performers leveraging the value-based incentive program to boost profitability.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

In North Dakota, this step is not about finding land; it’s about conducting thorough due diligence on a facility for acquisition. Your evaluation must go beyond the purchase price to assess the building’s physical condition, regulatory history, and potential for improvement. Key facility requirements you must assess include:

  • Compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and CMS’s Life Safety Code. Deficiencies here can require costly renovations.
  • Adequate resident rooms meeting state and federal square footage requirements, with accessible bathrooms.
  • A commercial-grade kitchen and dining areas that meet health department standards.
  • Designated, functional areas for therapy services, resident activities, and administrative offices.
  • Properly located nurse’s stations with secure medication storage and preparation areas.
  • Functional emergency power systems, fire alarms, and sprinkler systems.

Your location selection during acquisition should consider the facility’s existing reputation, proximity to hospital referral partners, and the availability of a qualified local workforce. An aging building with significant deferred maintenance can quickly erode the profitability of an otherwise attractive acquisition.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

Staffing is the single most important driver of quality care and regulatory compliance. A successful nursing facility in North Dakota requires a full team of dedicated professionals. Required roles typically include:

  • Licensed Nursing Home Administrator (LNHA): The overall manager of the facility, responsible for operations, finance, and regulatory compliance.
  • Director of Nursing (DON): An RN responsible for overseeing all clinical services and nursing staff.
  • Registered Nurses (RNs): Provide skilled nursing care, assessments, and supervision.
  • Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs): Administer medications and treatments under the supervision of an RN.
  • Certified Nursing Assistants (CNAs): Provide the majority of direct, hands-on care to residents.
  • Social Services Director: Manages resident psychosocial needs, admissions, and discharge planning.
  • Activities Director: Plans and implements a program of activities to meet residents’ social and recreational needs.
  • Dietary Manager & Staff: Responsible for all food service operations.
  • Housekeeping & Maintenance Staff: Ensure a clean, safe, and well-maintained environment.

Training is not a one-time event; it is an ongoing process. Mandatory training requirements include initial orientation on resident rights, abuse prevention, and infection control. All CNAs must complete a state-approved certification program. Furthermore, all licensed staff (RNs, LPNs, LNHA) must complete ongoing continuing education units (CEUs) to maintain their licenses. For facilities with specialized units, dementia-specific training is crucial for staff.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Written policies and procedures are the operational blueprint for your facility. They ensure consistency, guide staff actions, and are a primary focus of state and federal surveyors. When acquiring a facility, you will likely need to overhaul the existing policy manual to reflect your operational philosophy and current best practices. North Dakota requires written policies covering:

  • Resident Rights and Grievance Procedures
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Policies
  • Comprehensive Resident Assessment and Care Planning
  • Infection Prevention and Control (a major survey focus)
  • Medication Management and Administration
  • Staffing Plans and Training Programs
  • Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Planning
  • Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI)

Individual care plans are the cornerstone of resident-centered care. These plans must be developed by an interdisciplinary team based on a comprehensive assessment, reviewed regularly, and meticulously documented to comply with North Dakota and federal rules. A strong set of policies, combined with diligent care planning, is your best defense during an inspection.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

In the skilled nursing industry, marketing is not about consumer advertising; it’s about professional relationship building. Your primary referral sources are other healthcare providers who need to place patients in a post-acute or long-term care setting. Referrals typically come from:

  • Hospital discharge planners and case managers
  • Physician practices and specialty clinics
  • Home health agencies
  • Assisted living facilities (for residents whose care needs have increased)
  • Community-based social workers and elder care attorneys

Successful providers in North Dakota focus on building a reputation for compliance, clinical excellence, and responsiveness. Your ability to accept referrals quickly, communicate effectively with the referring entity, and produce positive patient outcomes (like low hospital readmission rates) is your most powerful marketing tool. Documenting your success through quality metrics is essential for becoming a preferred partner for local hospitals.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Oversight in North Dakota is continuous and rigorous. Inspections are conducted by surveyors from the ND Department of Health and Human Services (ND HHS), who also act on behalf of CMS for federal certification surveys. These unannounced inspections, known as surveys, are comprehensive and can last several days.

Inspections focus on a wide range of areas, but some of the most common deficiencies cited nationally and in North Dakota include:

  • Infection control practices (e.g., improper hand hygiene, PPE usage)
  • Accident prevention and resident supervision
  • Food safety, storage, and sanitation
  • Medication administration errors and improper storage
  • Incomplete, inaccurate, or outdated resident care plans
  • Failure to properly report and investigate allegations of abuse or neglect

Maintaining a state of continuous survey readiness is not optional. This requires a robust Quality Assurance and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program where you proactively identify risks, audit your own systems, and implement corrective action plans. Audit-ready documentation is essential to demonstrating your compliance to surveyors.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to open a Nursing Facility in North Dakota?

Due to the statewide moratorium on new beds, opening a new facility is not possible until at least July 2029. The viable path is acquiring an existing facility. This involves a Change of Ownership (CHOW) process, which includes state licensing and federal certification approvals that typically take 4 to 9 months to complete.

What licenses are required?

A Nursing Facility license from the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services (ND HHS) is the primary state license required. To serve the vast majority of residents, the facility must also be certified by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to accept Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement.

What reimbursement is available?

Reimbursement comes from three main sources: Medicare (primarily for short-term, post-acute rehabilitation stays), North Dakota Medicaid (the primary payer for long-term care residents), and private pay residents. North Dakota Medicaid offers specific rates, such as approximately $399.55/day for swing beds, and provides access to an $8 million annual pool for value-based purchasing incentives for high-performing facilities.

Conclusion

Starting a Nursing Facility in North Dakota is a venture for well-capitalized, experienced operators prepared for a complex regulatory environment. The moratorium on new construction makes the market a landscape of acquisition, where success hinges on improving existing facilities. It requires careful planning, a deep understanding of ND HHS and CMS regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. Providers who invest in compliance, specialized staff training, and strong clinical referral relationships are positioned for long-term success and sustainability in this stable, high-demand market.
